extracted.intended_audience: literate urban readers interested in manners, morals, and periodical essays (early-18th-century general readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative judgments relevant to composing or evaluating Spectator-style periodical essays and contributions, and to the social behaviours those essays judge (manners, temper, marriage, publishing practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage choice / matchmaking ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents and matchmakers should not sacrifice a child's endowments and qualifications to obtain wealth in marriage; imposing a poor or ignorant husband on an accomplished woman is an injustice that makes life 'lastingly unhappy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained through the figure of 'Sempronia' who arranges matches for money: she adorns worthless men with apparent estate, ignores disparity in sense/education, and treats defects as proofs of wealth. Anti-patterns: forcing a liberal, ingenious child into the arms of a clown or blockhead; preferring conspicuous wealth over genuine compatibility and the child's happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dress modesty / 'naked-shouldered' social norm
rubrics_metrics.description: Women ought not to expose more than the fore-part of the neck; excessive exposure (the 'naked shouldered') creates unnecessary rivals and social mischief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offered via a correspondent's animadversion: visible shoulders are said to provoke jealousy and competitive behaviour. The writer suggests limiting exposed dress to preserve civility and avoid creating 'rivals'—an implied style rule for fashionable conduct. (An allowance is suggested only for those defective in facial charms.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-command / containment of anger
rubrics_metrics.description: To contain the spirit of anger is the worthiest discipline: a man should master sudden inclinations to anger and exercise reason in moments of passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: quick sensibility often accompanies understanding, but reason should be called upon to master it. Examples of anti-patterns include public insults to family, assembling private allusions that dissolve peace, and theatrical madness (cited Nat Lee's 'Alexander'). Commendable example: great souls who conquer their natural anger (Lord Somers referenced). Practical advice: study to master anger for personal and social tranquility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of social tolerance for habitual humour
rubrics_metrics.description: No one ought to be tolerated in an habitual humour, whim, or particularity of behaviour by those who do not depend on him for their livelihood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains social boundary: dependents (those who 'wait upon him for Bread') may be obliged to bear eccentricities, but others should not endure habitual peevishness, snarliness, or continual ill manners. Anti-patterns: allowing a peevish or snarling person to disturb gatherings without consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of spies and secret intelligence (for rulers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers may need intelligence but must employ it cautiously and not rely unduly on secret informers, who are likely to inflame, aggravate, and misrepresent what they report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: spies lack honour and conscience and will often carry what is 'grateful' rather than true; they may let private spite enter their reports. Example: an Italian author's scene of a Cardinal and his spy—reports escalate until the patron is enraged. Practical implication: exercise prudence in accepting clandestine evidence and consider fairness to those accused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal indifference to slanders / avoid impertinent curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not be impertinently solicitous to know what is said of him in private; seeking out malicious reports torments the person and often makes matters worse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: the tongue is petulant and thoughts variable; praise and obloquy often come from the same mouth. Example: a great man who fretted over private expressions exposed himself and worsened his condition (Lord Treasurer Western). Advice: avoid officious friends who repeat malicious reports and do not let present speeches unduly affect you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial treatment of contributors' papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributions that are 'extremely natural and peculiarly good' should be printed entire and without alteration when changing them would 'do them a manifest Hurt and Violence'; editors may adapt other pieces to the paper's character, but must judge when to preserve native style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele's account: as project-editor he sometimes adapted others' papers into his style, but on review recognized that some writings must appear in their own 'native Dress and Colours.' Guidance for editors: balance adapting to the periodical's tone with respect for the contributor's voice; publish some 'Spectators' by other hands intact; temper editorial pride with humility ('An Author should take all Methods to humble himself').

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners in company (rules illustrated by the Infirmary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good company requires moderation of behaviour: insolence to servants, excessive sulkiness, persistent dullness, refusing convivial participation, loud clamorous argument, and rude physical gestures (thumping table) are grounds for exclusion from civil company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the fraternity's week of proceedings: offences leading to confinement in the 'Infirmary' include swearing at a servant, long fits of stupidity construed as contempt, constant fault-finding at table, inability to laugh, and raising voice to drown argument. Enforcement: the president maintains order; penalties include removal, confinement, diet with water-gruel, and temporarily excluding petitioners until they reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust in Providence as a practical virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: A steady trust in the Supreme Being produces patience, hope, cheerfulness, and practical strength in adversity; it is both a duty and of natural tendency to relieve affliction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: reliance on divine attributes supplies what human foresight and strength lack, encouraging fortitude 'in the Hour of Death' and in calamity. The essay offers a pastoral translation of David's twenty-third Psalm as a model of this disposition and its consolations.
